exercises.objective: Distinguish joint, marginal, and conditional probability.
exercises.prompt: For two random variables $X,Y$, explain in your own words the difference between the joint distribution $P(X,Y)$, the marginal $P(X)$, and the conditional $P(X\mid Y)$, and how the marginal and conditional are each obtained from the joint.
hints: $P(X,Y)$ describes the probability of $X$ and $Y$ taking specific values *together*, it's the most complete description of how the two variables relate.
The marginal $P(X)$ answers 'what's the probability of $X$, ignoring $Y$ entirely?' It's obtained by summing (or integrating) the joint over all values of $Y$: $P(X) = \sum_y P(X,y)$.

The conditional $P(X\mid Y=y)$ answers 'what's the probability of $X$, given that we've observed $Y=y$ specifically?' It's obtained by taking the joint's slice at $Y=y$ and renormalizing: $P(X\mid Y=y) = P(X,y)/P(y)$, dividing by $P(y)=\sum_x P(x,y)$ so the conditional sums to 1 over $X$.

exercises.objective: Derive Bayes' rule from the definition of conditional probability.
exercises.prompt: Starting from the definition $P(A\mid B) = P(A,B)/P(B)$ (and the symmetric $P(B\mid A)=P(A,B)/P(A)$), derive Bayes' rule: $P(A\mid B) = \dfrac{P(B\mid A)P(A)}{P(B)}$.
hints: Both definitions involve the same joint $P(A,B)$. Rearrange each to isolate $P(A,B)$.
From $P(A\mid B) = P(A,B)/P(B)$: $P(A,B) = P(A\mid B)P(B)$. From $P(B\mid A)=P(A,B)/P(A)$: $P(A,B) = P(B\mid A)P(A)$.
Since both expressions equal $P(A,B)$, set them equal: $P(A\mid B)P(B) = P(B\mid A)P(A)$. Dividing both sides by $P(B)$ gives Bayes' rule directly: $P(A\mid B) = P(B\mid A)P(A)/P(B)$.

exercises.objective: Apply Bayes' rule to compute a posterior probability.
exercises.prompt: A diagnostic test for a rare condition (prior prevalence $P(\text{disease})=0.02$) has $P(\text{positive}\mid\text{disease})=0.9$ (true positive rate) and $P(\text{positive}\mid\text{no disease})=0.1$ (false positive rate). Using Bayes' rule, compute $P(\text{disease}\mid\text{positive})$. Enter a decimal to 4 decimal places.
hints: First compute $P(\text{positive})$ via the law of total probability: $P(\text{pos}) = P(\text{pos}\mid\text{disease})P(\text{disease}) + P(\text{pos}\mid\text{no disease})P(\text{no disease})$.

$P(\text{disease}\mid\text{pos}) = \dfrac{P(\text{pos}\mid\text{disease})P(\text{disease})}{P(\text{pos})} = \dfrac{0.018}{0.116} \approx 0.1552$. Notice how low this is despite a 90% true-positive rate, a direct consequence of the disease being rare (a classic illustration of why the prior/base rate matters so much).

exercises.objective: Compute a marginal distribution from a joint distribution table.
exercises.prompt: A joint distribution $P(X,Y)$ over $X\in\{0,1\}$, $Y\in\{0,1,2\}$ is given by $P(X{=}0,Y{=}0)=0.1$, $P(X{=}0,Y{=}1)=0.2$, $P(X{=}0,Y{=}2)=0.05$, $P(X{=}1,Y{=}0)=0.15$, $P(X{=}1,Y{=}1)=0.3$, $P(X{=}1,Y{=}2)=0.2$ (these sum to 1). Compute the marginal $P(X{=}1)$. Enter a decimal.
hints: The marginal $P(X{=}1)$ sums the joint over all values of $Y$, at $X=1$: $P(X{=}1) = P(X{=}1,Y{=}0)+P(X{=}1,Y{=}1)+P(X{=}1,Y{=}2)$.
